Read About Jaipur

A city that was drawn on paper before a single wall of it stood, and painted a color it never wore before 1876.

A city planned before it was built

Most of India's old cities grew the way rivers do — a fort first, then a temple, then a market, then centuries of streets bending around whatever was already there. Jaipur did not. In 1727, Maharaja Sawai Jai Singh II — an astronomer as much as a king, and the same man who would go on to build the observatory at Jantar Mantar — decided his hilltop capital at Amber had run out of room and water, and commissioned an entirely new city on the plain below it. He handed the design to Vidyadhar Bhattacharya, a Bengali scholar of Shilpa Shastra, the ancient Hindu treatises on architecture and town planning, and the result was a nine-block grid based on the Prithvi Vastu Purusha Mandala, a cosmological diagram that treats a city as a body laid out in harmony with the sun's path. Broad avenues cross at right angles, block widths step down from the center outward, and the whole plan is enclosed by a fortified wall pierced with seven gates. It is one of the earliest planned cities in India, and unusually for a project this old, it was finished largely as drawn.

The whole plan is enclosed by a fortified wall pierced with seven gates — a city drawn as a diagram before it was built as a place.

The paint that gave the city its name

Jaipur's terracotta-pink walls are not the stone underneath — they are a coat of paint, and a comparatively recent one. In 1876, Maharaja Sawai Ram Singh II had the entire walled Old City whitewashed and then painted a warm pink to welcome the Prince of Wales, Albert Edward, on his tour of India — pink being a traditional color of hospitality in Rajasthani custom. The gesture stuck. A municipal ordinance still requires shopkeepers and residents inside the old walled city to keep their facades the same shade, which is why the color has survived a century and a half of repainting, monsoons and renovation largely unbroken, and why "Pink City" describes the historic core specifically rather than Jaipur as a whole.

A skyline of forts, laced together by a single wall

Amber Fort, Jaigarh Fort and Nahargarh Fort look, from below, like three separate hilltop monuments — but they were built as one connected defensive system. A single fortified wall, running along the Aravalli ridge above the old capital, links all three: Amber as the royal residence, Jaigarh as the garrison and arsenal directly above it, and Nahargarh further along the ridgeline as the outer watch-post overlooking the new city on the plain. The section of that same rampart road between Amber and Jaigarh is walkable today as a hiking trail, which means a visitor can, quite literally, follow the same stone path an 18th-century sentry would have walked between the two forts.

Jaigarh's contribution to that system was as much industrial as military: the fort housed its own cannon foundry, and in 1720 it cast the Jaivana, still recognized as the largest cannon ever built on wheels. Eight tonnes of bronze on an 8-foot barrel, the Jaivana was fired exactly once, as a test shot, reportedly sending its ball more than 30 kilometers and leaving a crater that later filled with water to form a lake. It has stood loaded with nothing but tourists' curiosity ever since.

Windows built for watching, not for being watched

Hawa Mahal — the "Palace of Winds" — is the building most people picture when they picture Jaipur, and its five-tier honeycomb facade of pink sandstone is almost entirely decorative: there is no grand hall behind it, just a narrow set of chambers one room deep. It was built in 1799 for a specific and practical purpose. Royal women of the Zenana, kept from appearing unveiled in public under the custom of purdah, could sit behind its 953 small latticed windows — jharokhas — and watch the processions and street life of the city below without ever being seen themselves. The lattice screens also work as a passive cooling system, drawing air through the narrow openings and across the chambers behind them, which is where the building's name actually comes from.

An observatory built by a king who did the math himself

Jantar Mantar, a short walk from the City Palace, is not a single structure but a working collection of nineteen astronomical instruments, all built from stone and marble rather than metal, and all still capable of the readings they were designed for. Jai Singh II built it between 1728 and 1734, one of five such observatories he commissioned across northern India, because he distrusted the imported European instruments and tables of his era and wanted measurements taken at a scale accurate enough to trust by eye. Its Samrat Yantra, a 27-metre equinoctial sundial, remains the largest sundial of its kind in the world and can still be read to an accuracy of about two seconds. UNESCO listed the site as a World Heritage property in 2010, citing it as the most comprehensive surviving example of the Ptolemaic positional astronomy several Asian civilizations shared before the arrival of telescopes.

A palace that is still, in part, a home

City Palace sits at the geometric and ceremonial center of Jai Singh II's original grid, and unlike most former royal residences on the guidebook circuit, it has never fully stopped being one. The former Jaipur royal family still occupies private apartments in the Chandra Mahal, the palace's central seven-storey building, and its museum wings — opened to the public — hold the royal collection of textiles, weaponry and manuscripts alongside a still-functioning silver-and-marble reception hall used for state occasions. The palace complex blends Rajput and Mughal architectural vocabulary in a way that was itself a political statement in the 18th century: a visible sign of the alliance between the Kachwaha Rajputs and the Mughal court that had made Jaipur's founding possible in the first place.
